orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, continuing her story to Lockwood. It is the evening after Edgar Linton's funeral, in early autumn 1801. Nelly and the newly married Cathy sit in the library at Thrushcross Grange, wondering what will become of them.

notes.g: Thinking sadly.
Daring to make guesses.
Go on living at the Grange.
notes.n: The Grange has passed to Linton, Edgar's heir, so it is now in Heathcliff's power.

notes.t: retaining my home and my employment
notes.g: Keeping my home and my job.
One of the servants who had been dismissed.
Who had not left yet.

notes.t: fasten the door in his face
notes.g: Lock the door against him.
Didn't bother with the politeness of knocking.
He was now in charge at the Grange.
notes.n: Linton has inherited the Grange, and Linton is under age and completely in his father's power. So in practice Heathcliff is master here now.

notes.t: availed himself of the master’s privilege
notes.g: Used the master's right.
The servant who had warned us.

notes.t: ushered, as a guest, eighteen years before
notes.g: Shown in as a visitor eighteen years ago.
notes.n: When Heathcliff came back and called on Catherine at the Grange (Chapter X).

notes.g: Paintings of Cathy's parents.
notes.n: Lockwood was shown Edgar's portrait in Chapter VIII.

notes.t: the splendid head of Mrs. Linton
notes.g: The portrait of Catherine, Edgar's wife and Cathy's mother.

notes.t: the graceful one of her husband
notes.g: The portrait of Edgar.
More yellowish and unhealthy-looking.
About 14 to 28 pounds heavier.
notes.n: A 'stone' is a British unit of weight equal to 14 pounds, still used for body weight.

notes.g: No more running away!
An obedient daughter.
notes.n: Heathcliff is now her father-in-law, and he means her to obey him.

notes.t: I was embarrassed how to punish him
notes.g: I was at a loss how to punish him.
notes.m: 'Embarrassed' meant puzzled or hampered, not ashamed.

notes.g: So flimsy and frail.
Got what he deserved.
Powerful in its effect on his nerves.
For hours at a time.
Your darling husband (said sarcastically).

notes.t: I yield all my interest in him to you
notes.g: I hand over all responsibility for him to you.

notes.t: a daily plague to your unnatural heart
notes.g: A daily nuisance to your cold, unfatherly heart.

notes.t: I’m seeking a tenant for the Grange
notes.g: I'm looking for someone to rent the Grange.
notes.n: Keep in mind who is renting Thrushcross Grange when the novel opens (Chapter I).

notes.t: owes me her services for her bread
notes.g: Must work for her keep.

notes.t: nurture her in luxury and idleness
notes.g: Keep her in comfort, doing nothing.

notes.t: don’t oblige me to compel you
notes.g: Don't force me to make you.
I dare you; I stand up to you.
A bragging defender.
Extremely bitter.
notes.n: Gall is bile, famously bitter. 'Gall' for bitterness appears often in the Bible.

notes.t: draw a pleasant picture to Zillah
notes.g: Describe to Zillah (said ironically: the picture was cruel).
He has the wish (to be cruel).

notes.t: Lonely, like the devil, and envious like him
notes.g: Cut off from love and envious of others' happiness, like Satan.
notes.n: In Christian tradition, Satan, thrown out of heaven, envies human happiness. Milton's 'Paradise Lost' famously shows him this way.

notes.g: A bleak, joyless sort of victory.

notes.t: enter into the spirit of her future family
notes.g: Take on the cruel ways of her new family.
Heathcliff, father of her husband Linton.
Very soon.
Go away, you witch.
Left the room with contempt.
Ask to take Zillah's job as housekeeper at the Heights.

notes.t: he would suffer it on no account
notes.g: He would not allow it at all.
notes.m: 'Suffer' here means allow, not feel pain.

notes.g: I'll take that portrait home with me.

notes.t: for lack of a better word
notes.g: Because there's no better word for it.
The church officer who looked after the churchyard and dug graves.
Edgar Linton's grave.
notes.n: In this speech 'Linton' means Edgar, not his son.

notes.g: The coffin of Catherine, Cathy's mother.
notes.n: Edgar's grave was dug beside hers (Chapter XVI).

notes.g: It still looks like her!
Not the side facing Edgar's grave.
notes.n: Catherine lies between Edgar and the spot Heathcliff means to have for himself. He has loosened the side of her coffin that faces his own future grave.

notes.g: Sealed inside a lead coffin.
notes.n: Wealthy people were sometimes buried in lead-lined coffins sealed with solder, which kept the body apart and slowed decay.

notes.g: Remove the matching side of my coffin too.
notes.n: So that, when both have decayed, their remains will mingle.

notes.t: he’ll not know which is which
notes.g: Edgar won't be able to tell Heathcliff's dust from Catherine's.
Interfere with a grave.
notes.n: Opening a grave was thought deeply wrong, and digging up a body was a crime.

notes.g: Last night.

notes.t: sleeping the last sleep by that sleeper
notes.g: Lying dead beside her.
Decayed into dust.

notes.t: such a transformation on raising the lid
notes.g: To find her body decayed when I lifted the lid.

notes.t: a distinct impression of her passionless features
notes.g: A clear sight of her calm, still face.

notes.t: I was wild after she died
notes.g: I was frantic after her death.

notes.t: praying her to return to me her spirit
notes.g: Begging her ghost to come back to me.
notes.n: Remember his wild prayer for her to haunt him, at the end of Chapter XVI.

notes.t: I have a strong faith in ghosts
notes.g: I firmly believe in ghosts.
notes.n: Think back to Lockwood's nightmare and Heathcliff's cry at the window in Chapter III.

notes.t: The day she was buried, there came a fall of snow
notes.g: The weather turned to snow after the funeral.
notes.n: This is the night Isabella described in Chapter XVII.

notes.g: The wind was as cold as winter.
About six feet of freshly dug soil.
The shed where tools are kept.
Dig.
Reaching my goal.
The wind full of sleet.
Something solid and real.
Here 'Cathy' means Catherine, young Cathy's mother.
notes.n: Heathcliff often called her Cathy.

notes.t: I relinquished my labour of agony
notes.g: I gave up my desperate digging.
Comforted beyond words.

notes.t: that accursed Earnshaw and my wife opposed my entrance
notes.g: Hindley and Isabella barred me from coming in.
notes.n: See Isabella's account of that night in Chapter XVII.

notes.t: I ought to have sweat blood
notes.g: I suffered such agony I should have sweated blood.
notes.n: An echo of Jesus praying in Gethsemane, whose 'sweat was as it were great drops of blood' (Luke 22:44).

notes.g: The passion of my pleading prayers.

notes.t: the sport of that intolerable torture
notes.g: The plaything of that unbearable torment.
Hellish!

notes.t: if they had not resembled catgut
notes.g: If they hadn't been as tough as catgut.
notes.n: Catgut is strong cord made from animal intestines, used for violin strings.

notes.t: when I slept in her chamber
notes.g: When I slept in her old bedroom.
notes.n: The room with the oak box-bed where Lockwood spent his night in Chapter III.

notes.t: I was beaten out of that
notes.g: I was driven out of there.
Opening the sliding panels of the box-bed.
notes.n: Lockwood's ghost dream happened in this same bed (Chapter III).

notes.g: It tortured me.
notes.n: The rack was an instrument of torture that stretched the body.

notes.g: Joseph, the old servant at the Heights.

notes.t: playing the fiend inside of me
notes.g: Tormenting me like a devil inside.
I'm calmed.

notes.t: not by inches, but by fractions of hairbreadths
notes.g: Not just slowly, but unbearably slowly.
notes.n: 'Killing by inches' meant a slow death. Heathcliff makes it even slower.

notes.t: beguile me with the spectre of a hope
notes.g: Tease me with the ghost of a hope.
Wet with sweat.
The glowing coals.

notes.t: the grim aspect of his countenance
notes.g: The grim look on his face.

notes.t: mental tension towards one absorbing subject
notes.g: A mind straining towards one thing that fills it.
I kept quiet.

notes.t: resumed his meditation on the picture
notes.g: Went back to gazing thoughtfully at the portrait.
Look at it more easily.
Send that portrait to the Heights tomorrow.
Her new father-in-law.
Your nosiness; your snooping.

notes.t: He signed her to precede him
notes.g: He signalled for her to walk ahead of him.
Resisted it.
A garden walk lined with trees.
notes.m: Not a narrow back street. An 'alley' was a path between trees or hedges in a garden.
